questions.question: Build the fixed assets note for the equipment and name its three agreements.
questions.expected_answer: Opening carrying value nil (bought this year); additions at cost R14 000; depreciation for the year R2 800; closing carrying value R11 200, presented as cost R14 000 less accumulated depreciation R2 800. Agreements: the closing carrying value equals the statement of financial position's fixed assets line; the year's depreciation charge equals the income statement's depreciation expense; and the asset register stands behind the note as the item-level detail.

questions.question: Build the four working-capital notes and the owner's equity note, with totals.
questions.expected_answer: Inventories: trading stock R10 700 + consumable stores on hand R400 = R11 100. Trade and other receivables: trade debtors R6 300 + accrued income R600 + prepaid expenses R1 200 = R8 100. Cash and cash equivalents: bank R24 500 + petty cash R450 + cash float R250 = R25 200. Trade and other payables: trade creditors R10 200 + accrued expenses R300 + income received in advance R600 = R11 100. Owner's equity: opening R22 000 + contributions nil + net profit R10 500 − drawings R4 500 = closing R28 000. Every total must agree with its statement line to the rand.

questions.question: Explain the connection between formal statements and indigenous bookkeeping.
questions.expected_answer: Stokvels, burial societies and savings clubs have kept trusted records for generations — contribution registers, member pages, payout rosters — sharing the same architecture as formal accounting: member-by-member detail agreeing with a running total (a control account and its list in another form) and full transparency to every stakeholder. Both traditions solve the universal problem that money held for others must be accounted to them in detail, on demand; GAAP and the stokvel book are two languages for the same honesty, and both punish a total that cannot survive the member's check.
